speaker: maya
text: Last time: the labor chain — encomienda, the repartimiento draft, African slavery, the casta ladder. Now the empire stops to argue with itself. Spain has conquered half a hemisphere, and in 1550 the crown puts its own conquests on trial: can conquest ever be just? Four boxes: Sepúlveda's case for natural slavery, Las Casas's answer, the New Laws and the verdict that wasn't, and the afterlife. Circle the ones you couldn't explain right now. Twelve and a half minutes. For the conquest: Sepúlveda, the court's scholar of Aristotle. Against it: Marcus, arguing Las Casas's case. I did mock trial in eighth grade, and my coach drilled one rule: a hung jury means nobody wins. Just saying.

speaker: maya
text: One note first: the quoted lines you'll hear are Las Casas's actual words. The debate around them is our dramatization.

speaker: maya
text: August 1550, Valladolid, Spain. The emperor Charles the Fifth has paused the conquests while his theologians and jurists hear two cases. For the conquest: Juan Ginés de Sepúlveda. Against it: Marcus, arguing the case of Bartolomé de las Casas — Dominican friar, decades in the Indies, former bishop of Chiapas. Sepúlveda, open your case.

speaker: sepúlveda
text: I argue from Aristotle, who wrote nearly two thousand years before any ship of ours crossed the ocean: some peoples are slaves by nature, born to be ruled, incapable of governing themselves. Oviedo's chronicles, the fruit of decades in the Indies, describe peoples who fit the account. They are homunculi, little men, in whom you will barely find the vestiges of humanity. Spanish rule is not cruelty. It is order, carried to those who cannot produce it for themselves.

speaker: maya
text: Homunculi. Wait, like the villains in Fullmetal Alchemist?

speaker: sepúlveda
text: I do not know your alchemists. In my Latin the word means little men.

speaker: marcus
text: You heard a cartoon word. He meant it as natural history, and that's the whole problem.

speaker: maya
text: Marcus, your answer.

speaker: marcus
text: His case starts with who counts as human. The peoples of the Indies are rational souls: capable of the Christian faith, and capable of governing themselves. They had towns and laws before they ever heard the word Spaniard. He argues from your own doctors: Aquinas taught that dominion comes from natural law, not from grace. Even unbelievers hold true title to their lands. Deny that, and you deny your own theology. His standing: he held an encomienda himself, and gave it back in a sermon in 1514.

speaker: maya
text: Round one: Sepúlveda's case. The four causes, laid out.

speaker: sepúlveda
text: Four just causes for war against them. Their natural condition, which makes them slaves by nature, whom it is just and useful to rule. Their idolatry and human sacrifice, which offend natural law itself, a law binding all peoples whether they acknowledge it or not. The innocent, dragged to their altars, crying out for rescue. And the faith, which they cannot receive unless we carry it to them. A war that ends such practices is an act of mercy. That is my case.

speaker: maya
text: First box on the table: natural slavery and the four just causes. Scoring move: when a stimulus hands you Aristotle on natural slavery, write Sepúlveda, the court scholar, not a conquistador. The exam pairs the theory with the theorist.

speaker: maya
text: So you sailed over, saw it for yourself, and came back convinced?

speaker: sepúlveda
text: I never crossed the Atlantic, and I won't hide it. I relied on the chronicles, above all Oviedo's. But my argument does not depend on which village I visited. It depends on Aristotle, on natural law, on what reason tells us about peoples given to idolatry and human sacrifice. Village reports vary; the principle holds regardless.

speaker: maya
text: The common mistake for box one: don't write that Sepúlveda argued from what he saw. Books, not voyages. Aristotle and Oviedo's chronicles.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. You're one of the theologians on the junta. Sepúlveda argues from Aristotle and Oviedo's books. Las Casas answers: he was there, he watched it happen. Books or eyewitness: which evidence do you trust?

speaker: maya
text: Most of you just picked the eyewitness. The theologians heard both and picked neither. First box checked: Sepúlveda's case.

speaker: marcus
text: He read a Greek philosopher who died two thousand years before Columbus sailed, and wrote off a hemisphere. That's not an argument. That's a permission slip with Latin on it.

speaker: maya
text: Round two: Las Casas's answer. The book.

speaker: marcus
text: He wrote it down. A Short Account of the Destruction of the Indies, finished in 1542, printed ten years later. Village by village: the mines, the forced labor. Testimony from a man who watched it happen, not a scholar who read about it.

speaker: maya
text: And the numbers in it? Three million on Hispaniola, down to a couple hundred?

speaker: marcus
text: His numbers are the warning label on his own book. He claimed Hispaniola went from over three million souls to barely two hundred. Modern estimates put the starting figure far lower, and most of the dying was disease. The cruelty was real. The millions were not.

speaker: maya
text: Watch the trap: if a question quotes Las Casas describing a massacre, the follow-up isn't asking whether he's lying. It's asking what the exaggeration was for. He was writing to move a king, not to file a census.

speaker: maya
text: Trap for box two: his Hispaniola numbers look quotable, and they're wrong. The cruelty holds; the arithmetic doesn't.

speaker: maya
text: One blind spot first. Early on, Las Casas proposed shipping enslaved Africans to spare the Indians. His own plan.

speaker: marcus
text: His own plan, and the worst page he ever wrote. In 1516 he told the crown to bring enslaved Africans instead of working Natives to death. Decades later he took it back: enslaving Africans was every bit as unjust, and he wasn't sure his good intentions would excuse him. If no people are natural slaves, it holds for Africans too, or it holds for no one.

speaker: maya
text: Las Casas's answer so far: rational souls, ordered states, the eyewitness book, and the blind spots he owned.

speaker: maya
text: One more push. Ordered states, excellent laws: did Las Casas ever paint them gentler than they were?

speaker: marcus
text: Perhaps he did. But what he saw was humanity enough. The question was never whether they were perfect. It was whether they were people.

speaker: maya
text: Before the verdict that wasn't: the fight on the ground. The New Laws.

speaker: marcus
text: 1542. The crown tried to wind the encomienda down: no new grants, and when a holder died, the grant went back to the crown instead of passing to his children. Las Casas pushed for exactly that. For once, the crown listened.

speaker: sepúlveda
text: And the men holding the grants revolted. In Peru, Gonzalo Pizarro raised an army of encomenderos against the viceroy sent to enforce the laws. An empire cannot be governed against the men who hold it.

speaker: marcus
text: Charles the Fifth blinked. In 1545 he revoked the inheritance ban, and the encomienda survived. The next year the rebels killed the king's own viceroy at Añaquito, in January 1546.

speaker: maya
text: Timing trap: the New Laws came in 1542, the debate in 1550. A question that puts the debate first is testing whether you know the failure came first. The debate was the crown's second try.

speaker: maya
text: So the crown tries the question a different way. Not with laws, with a debate.

speaker: marcus
text: August 1550. The junta meets at Valladolid: theologians, jurists, the empire's best minds. Las Casas's case took days to lay out. Sepúlveda answered from his Democrates Alter. Then the junta met again in April 1551.

speaker: maya
text: Your turn. You're the junta. Condemn the conquest, and you unwind Spain's title to half a hemisphere. Bless it, and you hand every conquistador a license. Is there a third option?

speaker: maya
text: There's. Hear both cases, thank everyone, and never rule. The junta scattered without a verdict, and both sides claimed they'd won.

speaker: maya
text: That covers the New Laws, the revolt, and the debate with no verdict. The common mistake, two for one: don't write that the New Laws ended the encomienda. They didn't. And don't write that either side won. The judges scattered.

speaker: maya
text: Last box: the afterlife. Marcus, the book he wrote to move a king.

speaker: marcus
text: It moved his enemies instead. Dutch printers ran his Short Account first: the first Dutch edition in 1578, dozens more before their war with Spain ended. Then London, 1583, printed to turn the Low Countries against Spain. The friar who fought the conquest armed Spain's rivals with their best weapon. What historians later called the Black Legend: Spain the cruel tyrant, proven from a Spaniard's own pages, by men who cared nothing for the Indians.

speaker: maya
text: So he wrote it to save the Indians, and it became Protestant propaganda.

speaker: marcus
text: He wanted reform. He got a weapon, aimed at his own country.

speaker: maya
text: The common mistake for box four: students always credit Las Casas with inventing the Black Legend. English and Dutch printers built it from his pages: his reform book, turned into their propaganda.

speaker: maya
text: But the question outlived the book's misuse. Before Valladolid, had any empire ever put its own conquests on trial?

speaker: marcus
text: One historian called it the only time a mighty emperor ever halted his conquests to ask whether they were just. The junta never ruled. But the question survived: can a universal moral law judge a conqueror? Historians see that question as one seed of the natural-rights language that would outlive every empire here.

speaker: maya
text: Four boxes, let's land them. One: Sepúlveda's case. Aristotle's natural slaves, and the four just causes: natural slavery, idolatry and sacrifice offending nature, rescue of the innocents, and bringing the faith.

speaker: sepúlveda
text: One case, four causes: conquest as mercy.

speaker: maya
text: Box one, checked. Two: Las Casas's answer. Rational souls, ordered states, the Short Account, finished 1542, printed 1552. His numbers were exaggerated, his blind spots owned, his case unchanged: offer the faith, never force it.

speaker: marcus
text: And the encomienda he gave back in 1514.

speaker: maya
text: Right. Box two, checked. Three: the New Laws, 1542. No inheritance, dead on arrival. The crown revoked the ban in 1545, and the viceroy died at Añaquito in... 1546?

speaker: marcus
text: January 1546. Then the junta: August 1550, April 1551, no verdict.

speaker: maya
text: No verdict, both sides claiming victory. Box three, checked. Four: the afterlife. The Short Account becomes the Black Legend in English and Dutch hands, and the question becomes a seed of natural-rights talk. Lost the policy —

speaker: marcus
text: won the afterlife.

speaker: maya
text: Three questions, AP-shaped. Say your answer before I give it. And on the long essay: any prompt about whether the Spanish conquest was justified, this debate is your counterargument paragraph. State the strongest case for the conquest, then answer it with Las Casas. Graders reward the student who sees both sides.

speaker: maya
text: One, and it comes with a source. Las Casas, 1550: "They are not ignorant, inhuman, or bestial. Rather, long before they had heard the word Spaniard they had properly organized states, wisely ordered by excellent laws, religion, and custom." What is he claiming, and whose argument is he answering?

speaker: maya
text: Claim: the Native peoples are rational and self-governing. Evidence: ordered states, excellent laws, religion, custom, all before contact. Reasoning: a people who govern themselves can't be natural slaves. He's answering Sepúlveda.

speaker: maya
text: Two. A student writes: "Sepúlveda defended the conquest because he'd seen the Indies himself." What's the mistake?

speaker: maya
text: Claim: he never went. Evidence: he never crossed the Atlantic; his case came from Aristotle and Oviedo's chronicles. Reasoning: flip the expectation: the eyewitness case belonged to the side arguing against conquest, while the defense of conquest never left the library.

speaker: maya
text: Three. The junta heard both cases in 1550 and 1551, and never ruled. Why was a ruling dangerous either way?

speaker: maya
text: Claim: either verdict broke something. Evidence: condemn the conquest, and Spain's title to half a hemisphere unwinds; bless it, and every conquistador gets a license. Reasoning: so the junta scattered, and both sides claimed victory.

speaker: maya
text: One more, fast. Whose pages built the Black Legend, and whose presses printed it?

speaker: maya
text: Las Casas's pages. English and Dutch presses.

speaker: maya
text: Carry this one out the door: the empire put its own conquests on trial — and the trial outlived the empire. Check your four boxes. Next time: 1680, New Mexico. The Pueblos rise up and drive the Spanish out, and hold them out for over a decade.
